alerts.alert: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
alerts.name: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
alerts.desc: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files.
alerts.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to set the Content-Security-Policy header.

alerts.name: Hash Disclosure - SHA-256
alerts.desc: A hash was disclosed by the web server. - SHA-256
alerts.solution: Ensure that hashes that are used to protect credentials or other resources are not leaked by the web server or database. There is typically no requirement for password hashes to be accessible to the web browser.

alerts.alert: Server Leaks Information via "X-Powered-By" HTTP Response Header Field(s)
alerts.name: Server Leaks Information via "X-Powered-By" HTTP Response Header Field(s)
alerts.desc: The web/application server is leaking information via one or more "X-Powered-By" HTTP response headers. Access to such information may facilitate attackers identifying other frameworks/components your web application is reliant upon and the vulnerabilities such components may be subject to.
alerts.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to suppress "X-Powered-By" headers.

alerts.name: Charset Mismatch (Meta Content-Type Charset Missing)
alerts.desc:
This check identifies responses where the HTTP Content-Type header declares a charset different from the charset defined by the body of the HTML or XML. When there's a charset mismatch between the HTTP header and content body Web browsers can be forced into an undesirable content-sniffing mode to determine the content's correct character set.

An attacker could manipulate content on the page to be interpreted in an encoding of their choice. For example, if an attacker can control content at the beginning of the page, they could inject script using UTF-7 encoded text and manipulate some browsers into interpreting that text.

instances.otherinfo: Charset is defined only by META charset, older clients that expect character set to be defined by META content-type may not correctly display this content.

alerts.solution: Force UTF-8 for all text content in both the HTTP header and meta tags in HTML or encoding declarations in XML.
alerts.otherinfo: Charset is defined only by META charset, older clients that expect character set to be defined by META content-type may not correctly display this content.

alerts.name: Information Disclosure - Suspicious Comments
alerts.desc: The response appears to contain suspicious comments which may help an attacker. Note: Matches made within script blocks or files are against the entire content not only comments.

instances.otherinfo: The following pattern was used: \bUSER\b and was detected in the element starting with: "<script type="application/json" data-drupal-selector="drupal-settings-json">{"path":{"baseUrl":"\/","scriptPath":null,"pathPrefi", see evidence field for the suspicious comment/snippet.

alerts.solution: Remove all comments that return information that may help an attacker and fix any underlying problems they refer to.
alerts.otherinfo: The following pattern was used: \bUSER\b and was detected in the element starting with: "

alerts.name: Modern Web Application
alerts.desc: The application appears to be a modern web application. If you need to explore it automatically then the Ajax Spider may well be more effective than the standard one.

instances.otherinfo: Links have been found that do not have traditional href attributes, which is an indication that this is a modern web application.

alerts.solution: This is an informational alert and so no changes are required.
alerts.otherinfo: Links have been found that do not have traditional href attributes, which is an indication that this is a modern web application.

alerts.name: Re-examine Cache-control Directives
alerts.desc: The cache-control header has not been set properly or is missing, allowing the browser and proxies to cache content. For static assets like css, js, or image files this might be intended, however, the resources should be reviewed to ensure that no sensitive content will be cached.
alerts.solution: For secure content, ensure the cache-control HTTP header is set with "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate". If an asset should be cached consider setting the directives "public, max-age, immutable".

alerts.name: Retrieved from Cache
alerts.desc: The content was retrieved from a shared cache. If the response data is sensitive, personal or user-specific, this may result in sensitive information being leaked. In some cases, this may even result in a user gaining complete control of the session of another user, depending on the configuration of the caching components in use in their environment. This is primarily an issue where caching servers such as "proxy" caches are configured on the local network. This configuration is typically found in corporate or educational environments, for instance.

instances.otherinfo: The presence of the 'Age' header indicates that a HTTP/1.1 compliant caching server is in use.

alerts.solution:
Validate that the response does not contain sensitive, personal or user-specific information. If it does, consider the use of the following HTTP response headers, to limit, or prevent the content being stored and retrieved from the cache by another user:

Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private

Pragma: no-cache

Expires: 0

This configuration directs both HTTP 1.0 and HTTP 1.1 compliant caching servers to not store the response, and to not retrieve the response (without validation) from the cache, in response to a similar request.
alerts.otherinfo: The presence of the 'Age' header indicates that a HTTP/1.1 compliant caching server is in use.

alerts.alert: Server Leaks its Webserver Application via "Server" HTTP Response Header Field
alerts.name: Server Leaks its Webserver Application via "Server" HTTP Response Header Field
alerts.desc: The web/application server is leaking the application it uses as a webserver via the "Server" HTTP response header. Access to such information may facilitate attackers identifying other vulnerabilities your web/application server is subject to. This information alone, i.e. without a version string, is not very dangerous for the security of a server, nevertheless this information in the response header field is almost always useless and thus just an obsolete attacking vector.
alerts.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to suppress the "Server" header or provide generic details.
